newsitem.title: UK: British authorities discuss monetary policy.
newsitem.headline: British authorities discuss monetary policy.

text.p: Britain's finance minister Kenneth Clarke met Bank of England Governor Eddie George on Wednesday for their monthly meeting on monetary policy, but they made no announcement on interest rates.
Because Wednesday's meeting began after the central bank had concluded its daily money market operations, any decision on interest rates was unlikely to be announced until Thursday morning.
The Bank, which advises Clarke on monetary policy, has publicly called for official rates to be increased from the present 6.0 percent to prevent inflation taking off again.

But City economists expected Clarke, the Chancellor of the Exchequer, to leave rates unchanged this month, citing an unexpected drop in December manufacturing output and an apparent slowdown in consumer spending as evidence that there was no risk of the economy overheating.
A Reuters poll of 20 economists last week showed 12 expected no change in official rates.

Economists said an unexpectedly large drop of 45,100 in December UK unemployment, announced on Wednesday, suggested economic activity remained robust, but the figures would not materially alter the interest rate debate.
Average earnings growth was steady at 4.0 percent in the year to November, suggesting wage cost pressures remained under control.
"On balance these figures support the view that the economy is growing above trend," said Michael Saunders, an economist at Salomon Brothers.

"This argues in favour of a rate rise at some stage, either this month or later on. However, the slower pace of decline in unemployment shown by the Labour Force Survey should help reduce worries that the labour market already has tightened excessively."
Alex Garrard, an economist at UBS, said the jobs data were sufficiently ambiguous for Clarke to justfy leaving rates on hold for the time being.
"The next meeting is just three weeks away, by which time a clearer picture will have emerged about activity in the final three months of the year," he said.

The Conservative government faces an election by May and is reluctant to increase interest rates in the meantime as this would mean dearer home loans for millions of Britons with variable-rate mortgages.
